title: When and How Is the Internet Likely to Decrease Price Competition?
abstract: We challenge the assumption that the Internet intensifies price competition. Instead, we develop conditions under which the Internet may decrease competition. We develop an analytic model showing that the introduction of the Internet might lead to monopoly pricing when (1) the proportion of Internet users is high enough, (2) when nondigital attributes are relevant but not overwhelming, (3) when consumers have a more favorable prior about the brand they currently own, and (4) when the purchase situation can be characterized by 'destination shopping'. The Internet can increase consumer loyalty by raising effective search costs for products requiring physical inspection. The paper concludes that stores may become more important for customer acquisition while the Internet handles demand fulfillment for certain product categories.
summary_en: It was widely assumed in the late 1990s that the internet would intensify price competition by lowering search costs. Lal and Sárváry argue the opposite can happen: when products have both 'digital' attributes (easily described online) and 'nondigital' attributes (requiring physical inspection), heavy internet adoption can soften price competition by making consumers stickier to brands they already know. Their analytic model shows that internet diffusion above a threshold can produce monopoly-like pricing rather than the predicted price war, with stores remaining important for customer acquisition.
data_used: Theoretical model — no dataset. The model considers two competing brands, consumers with priors about non-digital product attributes, and a hybrid retail-internet distribution channel; comparative statics on price competition derived analytically.
policy_relevance: Hungarian competition policy (GVH) routinely assumes that e-commerce intensifies price competition. The paper provides a theoretical caveat: for product categories with high non-digital content (clothes, furniture, fresh food), e-commerce can soften price competition rather than tighten it. Useful for the GVH and the National Trade Council when assessing retail-market mergers and digital-marketplace dominance cases.
